segments.text: Harbor Learning Circle has three neat classroom briefs on a table.
All three were produced on time.
Morgan looks past the count.
One brief treats an unconfirmed facilitator as confirmed.
Another stopped because the note was stale.
The third accurately says the facilitator is still under review.
Three drafts tell Morgan very little about whether this work helps the team.
Last lesson gave us a contract and three test cases.
This lesson asks what we would watch over time and what Morgan must see before signing a decision.
Chapter 15 lays out seven rungs.
Activity, output, quality, behavior, outcome, learning, and authority.
A count of briefs belongs low on the latter.
For Harbor, quality asks whether each sentence is supported by a permitted, current source.
Behavior asks whether the preparer stopped at a stale note and respected the preparer-only gate.
Outcome asks whether Morgan could decide with less reconstruction and no hidden staffing claim.
Learning asks whether a revised contract reduces the same error in later approved tests.
Authority records the human-granted scope.
It is not a prize for a high count.
The workbook adds cost and trust to the scorecard.
Harbor can record course minutes for Morgan's review and an illustrative preparation cost
but cannot claim real savings.
For the paper case, the useful measures are source supported claims, correct holds,
Morgan's review burden, and whether a decision becomes clearer.
Write a decision beside each measure.
If a measure cannot tell Morgan to keep, revise, narrow, or stop the design,
take it off the front page.
Three classroom cases are a test exercise, not a performance baseline.
Chapter 16 asks us to choose a review posture for each action.
Pre-action review means the work waits for a human before a side effect.
Bounded action means a specifically fenced action may happen inside an already approved scope.
Post-action audit checks low stakes action after it happens, with a way to tighten the fence.
In this course, these are design choices on paper.
Harbor's brief may be prepared for Morgan.
Proposing a session, announcing it, booking a room,
or spending would need its own explicit human gate.
Nothing in our evaluation grants those permissions.
Give Morgan a review view that answers four questions.
What changed?
Which sources support it?
What is uncertain?
And what happens if Morgan says yes?
Make reject and request revision as visible as approved.
The stale facilitator note should land as a hold with a next step, not a green badge.
A reviewer who sees only a score will learn to clear a queue.
A reviewer who sees the evidence can take responsibility for a decision.
Pause.
Which number would make Harbor look busy while hiding the unsupported facilitator claim?
Add an agent metrics ladder and review postures card to your operating file.
Name one measure for activity, quality, behavior or trust, cost, and outcome.
Give each a source, a review cadence, a name decider, and the decision it could change.
Mark any unavailable baseline as unproven.
Then, classify three Harbor actions.
Drafting the brief, Morgan's internal review, and a proposed external announcement.
For each, state the reviewer view and stop condition.
Use a fictional or approved example.
Do not use private operational data or paste live dashboards or customer results.
Save revision nine as a draft.
The scorecard may tell Morgan where to look.
It does not sign for Morgan.
Next, we will put the same discipline around money and the final decision brief.
